content: Prunus africana, also known as Pygeum africanum (commonly referred to as pygeum), has specific dosing recommendations based on its intended use. It has traditionally been utilized for conditions such as inflammation, kidney disease, urinary problems, malaria, stomachache, fever, difficulty with urination, mental disturbances, and inflammation of the prostate gland. Pygeum is considered likely effective for alleviating symptoms of benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH), although it may be less effective compared to saw palmetto. Clinical evidence suggests that pygeum can reduce functional symptoms of BPH, including a 19% reduction in nocturia (frequent nighttime urination), a 23% increase in peak urine flow, and a 24% reduction in residual urine volume in men with BPH. Adverse effects associated with pygeum include nausea, abdominal pain, and hypersensitivity reactions. There is no established pregnancy category or lactation safety data for pygeum. However, in general, it is considered acceptable for use during pregnancy, as controlled studies in pregnant women have not demonstrated evidence of fetal risk. Information regarding its metabolism and excretion is not available. Pygeum contains active compounds such as ferulic acid, which has been shown to reduce prostatic cholesterol levels, and phytosterols, which inhibit prostaglandin synthesis. These mechanisms may contribute to its therapeutic effects in managing BPH symptoms.
